idiom_name: type sets + interface constraints (one code path for all permitted types); no specialization
implementation_notes: Go has neither overloading nor generic methods, and the generics design states explicitly that specialized implementations of polymorphic definitions are not a goal; inside a generic function only operations permitted by every type in the constraint's type set may be used, so a type parameter can never select an implementation. What replaces the classic structure: constraints (interface method sets, and type sets such as ~int | ~float64) let one algorithm serve many types; per-type behaviour is reached at run time through an interface value (itab dispatch) or, for closed sets, through a type switch or a map from tag to func value. The classic form is not applicable, and hand-written tables are justified only when the tag is a value you already carry.
pitfalls: Wanting specialization leads to type switches over every instantiation, which is exactly the pattern Go makes you pay for at run time (the community workaround described in golang/go#50681); the switch also cannot be checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler.
Pushing per-type behaviour towards constraints means every type must implement the methods, i.e. intrusive change on the types instead of a non-intrusive trait mapping.
Interface dispatch is not free and blocks inlining across the call, so a hot loop that used an interface to imitate a compile-time ladder keeps the cost the pattern exists to remove.
sources: The Go Blog, An Introduction To Generics (constraints as type sets; generic code may only use operations permitted by the constraint), https://go.dev/blog/intro-generics
Go Generics design draft: 'It is also not a goal to enable specialized implementations of polymorphic definitions', https://github.com/golang/proposal/blob/master/design/go2draft-generics-overview.md
golang/go issue #50681 (why per-instantiation dispatch inside a non-generic function is infeasible), https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50681
alternative: Express the property as a constraint (interface method set or type set such as ~int | ~float64) and write one implementation that every permitted type supports; where behaviour genuinely differs per type, use an interface with dynamic dispatch, or - for a closed set - a type switch or a table of func values keyed by a runtime tag. Go deliberately provides no specialization hook, so a per-type code path must be paid for with a runtime check.
